content: A nurse practitioner (NP) is a registered nurse (RN) who has undergone advanced education, typically at the master’s level, and specialized training in diagnosing and managing common medical conditions. NPs deliver a wide range of healthcare services, often similar to those provided by physicians, particularly in their areas of specialization, such as family practice, urgent care, or rural health. They work collaboratively with physicians and are licensed by the state in which they practice. NPs also hold board certifications, often through organizations like the American Nurses Credentialing Center (ANCC) or the National Certification Corporation (NCC) for specialty areas. NPs specialize in fields such as pediatrics, geriatrics, family medicine, psychiatry, and acute care. They manage both acute and chronic conditions by prescribing medications, ordering diagnostic tests, and initiating therapies. Many NPs are authorized to prescribe controlled substances and possess a DEA registration number. They can bill Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurance for their services. Depending on their scope of practice, NPs can serve as primary care providers for patients of all ages. Their approach emphasizes individualized care, focusing on the patient’s condition and the broader impact of illness on the patient and their family. NPs prioritize patient education and shared decision-making in healthcare. In some states, such as Oregon, Washington, and New Hampshire, NPs practice independently and may establish their own clinics. However, in 28 states, they are required to collaborate with or work under the supervision of a physician, although they can prescribe medications in all U.S. states and territories. The scope of practice for NPs varies by state but generally includes diagnosing, treating, and managing non-life-threatening acute and chronic illnesses, such as diabetes or hypertension. They take medical histories, perform physical exams, and order or interpret diagnostic tests like lab work, X-rays, or EKGs. NPs can prescribe medications, physical therapy, and rehabilitation treatments. They provide prenatal care, family planning, well-child care, immunizations, and health maintenance services for adults, including annual physicals. In acute and critical care settings, NPs may perform minor surgical procedures, such as biopsies, suturing, or casting, often with additional training and supervision. They collaborate with other healthcare professionals, provide referrals, and counsel patients on health behaviors, self-care, and treatment options. Some NPs are trained to act as surgical first assistants in operating rooms. NPs work in diverse settings, including community clinics, health departments, hospitals, urgent care centers, nursing homes, hospice centers, schools, and Veterans Administration facilities. They may also practice in private offices, public health departments, or walk-in clinics. To become an NP, one must first qualify as an RN, which requires completing an associate degree in nursing (ADN), a Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BSN), or a diploma program, along with direct patient care experience. ADN programs typically take two years, while BSN programs require four years. Most states mandate a master’s degree for NPs. Nurses with an ADN or diploma can pursue bridge programs to earn a BSN and master’s degree simultaneously. After becoming an RN, candidates must complete a state-approved advanced nursing education program, often specializing in areas like family practice, adult health, or women’s health. These programs grant either a Master of Science in Nursing (MSN) or a doctorate in nursing. The NP profession originated in 1965, initially requiring a master’s degree. During the 1970s, continuing education programs were introduced to meet the growing demand for NPs. Today, a master’s degree is the minimum requirement for new NPs, although those with prior qualifications were grandfathered in. NPs may also pursue national certification through organizations such as the American Association of Critical-Care Nurses or the National Certification Corporation for Obstetric, Gynecologic, and Neonatal Nursing Specialties. Some NPs obtain additional certifications in specialties like oncology, psychiatry, or emergency nursing. NPs use various post-nominal initials to indicate their qualifications and certifications. Examples include NP-C (Nurse Practitioner-Certified), APRN, BC (Advanced Practice Registered Nurse, Board Certified), and CNP (Certified Nurse Practitioner). Specialty-specific initials include ACNP (Acute Care Nurse Practitioner), FNP (Family Nurse Practitioner), PNP (Pediatric Nurse Practitioner), and WHNP (Women’s Health Nurse Practitioner). Advanced degrees and certifications, such as MSN (Master of Science in Nursing), DNP (Doctor of Nursing Practice), or FAANP (Fellow of the American Academy of Nurse Practitioners), may also be listed.
